title: Government Promotes Discussion to Regulate Social Media for Minors
author: Fernanda Monroy
content:
_This article by Fernanda Monroy originally appeared in the[July 27, 2026
edition of Contralínea](https://contralinea.com.mx/interno/semana/impulsa-
gobierno-discusion-para-regular-redes-sociales-en-menores/), a Mexican
investigative journalism magazine._

The federal government will promote a discussion to regulate access to social
media by girls, boys, and adolescents, after specialists warned that excessive
use of these platforms can affect brain development, attention, sleep, and
mental health during key stages of growth.

During the morning press conference, the Secretary of Public Education, Mario
Delgado Carrillo, explained that the initiative seeks to open a public debate
grounded in scientific evidence so that mothers, fathers, teachers, and
authorities know the risks associated with excessive use of devices and
digital platforms by minors.

The SEP head noted that** "the most important thing is that we are all taking
on this challenge together. The objective is for us to accompany this
generation and give them tools for a full and happy life."**

As part of that discussion, specialists in neurodevelopment and addiction
prevention presented research on the way social media and other digital
platforms interact with the brain during childhood and adolescence.

The general director of Concieo AC (an association to prevent addictions in
girls, boys, and young people), Tania Jiménez García, explained that
problematic technology use provokes an elevated release of dopamine, a
neurotransmitter related to the sensation of reward. Faced with that
overstimulation, she said, the brain reduces its production of this substance
and modifies its receptors as a protection mechanism, which can cause everyday
activities to stop generating satisfaction and favor the constant search for
digital stimuli.

The specialist added that this type of use can also affect functions such as
attention, concentration, impulse control, and emotional regulation. However,
she clarified that **the brain retains the capacity to recover through
neuroplasticity, as long as there is timely intervention and healthy habits.**

For her part, the director of the Center for Digital Youth at the University
of Washington, Lucía Magis Weinberg, explained that adolescence, between the
ages of 10 and 25, is a stage of intense brain reorganization. She indicated
that the regions related to emotions and reward-seeking mature before those in
charge of self-control and decision-making, which makes adolescents more
vulnerable to developing unhealthy habits.

The researcher noted that various studies show that constant use of digital
platforms can erode attention capacity. As an example, she indicated that two
decades ago a person could maintain concentration for around two and a half
minutes in front of a screen before getting distracted, while currently that
time has been reduced to approximately 47 seconds. She also warned that
increasingly early access to cell phones is associated with impacts on
cognitive development.

The specialist added that excessive screen use can also displace activities
essential for development, such as sleep, physical activity, in-person
socializing, and the construction of identity during adolescence, so she
recommended setting limits, promoting disconnection spaces, and strengthening
education for healthy technology use.

For her part,**President Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo affirmed that the federal
government is preparing informational materials directed at mothers and
fathers to spread awareness of the risks of excessive social media use, and to
foster decisions oriented toward protecting girls, boys, and adolescents.**

She also warned that, if this phenomenon is not addressed, the consequences
could impact not only the individual development of the new generations, but
also that of the country, so she stressed the importance of the discussion.
